title: Scaling, Failure, and Capacity Controls
summary: Scale self-hosted inference from measured demand while preserving quality, admission, failure isolation, availability, cost, and recovery evidence.
objectives: Choose vertical, replica, sharded, queued, cached, and routed scaling patterns from measured bottlenecks and failure domains.
Design admission, backpressure, load shedding, retry, timeout, circuit, and degraded-mode behavior before adding capacity.
Validate placement, warm-up, draining, autoscaling, shared-resource contention, and failure isolation.
Issue a scale decision with service, quality, cost, recovery, and rollback gates.

sections.title: Scale the measured bottleneck, not the diagram
paragraphs: Instructor narration: Begin with measurements, not a preferred topology. Inspect latency distributions, queue time, utilization, memory headroom, bandwidth, cache behavior, request sizes, concurrency, rejection, quality, and cost to identify the limiting resource. Possible responses include a larger device or host, more replicas, model or tensor parallelism, request batching, a bounded queue, caching, workload routing, or a smaller evaluated model. MLPerf Inference Datacenter illustrates why comparisons need defined workloads, scenarios, and measured systems. It supplies no measurement or score for this fictional exercise.

Worked synthetic bottleneck: Four ready replicas each complete 2 work units per interval, so ready capacity is 4 × 2 = 8 work units. Burst demand is 13. Queue delay rises from 20 ms to 410 ms while device utilization is 91 percent, memory headroom is 34 percent, artifact-store latency is 18 ms, and cache hit rate is 62 percent. These fictional teaching observations identify serving-compute throughput as the measured burst bottleneck. Thirteen demanded units minus eight immediately serviceable units leaves five units for queueing or rejection. A queue limited to two can absorb two, so three must be rejected under the baseline.

Eight alternatives and their tradeoffs: (1) Vertical scaling may increase throughput, but raises unit cost and host blast radius. (2) Additional replicas increase capacity only after readiness and only improve host availability when spread across failure domains. (3) Model or tensor parallelism may fit or accelerate a model, but adds communication and can widen the serving-unit failure domain. (4) Batching may improve utilization, but adds waiting time and requires evaluated batch limits. (5) A bounded queue absorbs a short burst, but creates no throughput and must fit the deadline. (6) Caching may remove repeated work, but requires correct identity, tenant isolation, freshness, and invalidation. (7) Workload routing can protect interactive traffic, but introduces a routing dependency and reserved-capacity tradeoffs. (8) A smaller model may reduce latency and cost, but requires a separate workload-specific quality and safety evaluation.

Worked decision: Add two warmed replicas to raise ready capacity from 8 to 12 work units, place them in a second host domain, retain a queue limit of two, and reject excess work before completion becomes impossible. Do not choose sharding because the model already fits with 34 percent synthetic memory headroom. Do not claim caching solves the burst because 38 percent of requests are misses. Retain only the previously evaluated batch bound. The design remains provisional until service, quality, placement, startup, failure, cost, recovery, and rollback gates pass.

Broad ecosystem transfer: Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Microsoft Phi, and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM may appear in self-hosted deployments, but model family, weights, runtime, serving API, and orchestration layer are distinct choices. Memory formats, licenses, prompt contracts, parallelism, compatibility, and security controls require separate verification. Do not infer equivalent capabilities across families or assume that one runtime supports every family. Official repositories used for transfer research are https://github.com/meta-llama/llama-models, https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen, https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3, https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-inference, https://github.com/microsoft/PhiCookBook, and https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM.

Learner activity: Before reading the worked artifact, identify the bottleneck and rank all eight alternatives. Connect each ranking to latency, quality, failure scope, cost, and complexity. Then repair the focused simulator defect. The broad design exercise is not reduced to that predicate. The predicate demonstrates one causal requirement within the larger policy: only ready, non-draining capacity can support admission.

sections.title: Control admission and backpressure
paragraphs: Instructor narration: Capacity does not replace admission control. Set request-body, context, output, concurrency, rate, queue, deadline, and resource limits by workload and priority. Reject early with stable retry guidance when work cannot complete inside its budget. Propagate deadlines and cancellation through the gateway, queue, server, runtime, and dependent tools. Backpressure prevents upstream demand from becoming unbounded downstream work.

Synthetic per-workload policy: Interactive requests permit a 1 MiB body, 8,192 context tokens, 1,024 output tokens, 16 concurrent requests per tenant, 20 requests per second, a queue of 2 work units, and a 1,000 ms deadline. Batch requests permit a 4 MiB body, 16,384 context tokens, 2,048 output tokens, 4 concurrent jobs per tenant, 2 jobs per second, a queue of 8 work units, and a 30,000 ms deadline. Administrative evaluation permits 2 concurrent jobs and no retry by default. These are fictional teaching limits, not production recommendations.

Retry and cancellation rules: Retry at most twice with bounded jitter, only for classified transient failures, only when repetition is safe, and always within the original deadline and queue budget. Never retry malformed input, authorization denial, deadline exhaustion, an unverified model, or a deterministic context-limit failure. Cancellation removes queued work and signals active work through each supported layer. If the runtime cannot stop active computation, suppress the result and account for residual capacity consumption.

Circuit, shedding, and degraded-mode rules: Open the artifact-store circuit after three classified failures within a 30-second exercise window. Allow one probe after a 20-second cooldown and close after two successful probes. Shed batch work first when ready capacity and its bounded queue cannot satisfy deadlines. Reject lower-priority interactive work next with retry guidance. A degraded mode may lower output limits to 256 tokens or use a separately evaluated fallback. It must not silently change model identity, weaken authorization, or claim equivalent quality without measurement.

Causal feedback: Deny-all is not a repair because it destroys available service and fails the positive changed-input case. Admit-all is also invalid because warming, draining, and failed replicas are fictional capacity. A valid decision requires ready capacity plus the bounded queue to cover demand, queue delay plus service time to fit the deadline, enough ready failure domains, and cost at or below its ceiling.

sections.title: Place, warm, drain, and replace capacity deliberately
paragraphs: Instructor narration: Schedule against actual device, memory, topology, storage, network, and driver requirements. Kubernetes resource requests influence placement and limits bound consumption. Extended devices such as GPUs cannot be overcommitted in the same way as fractional CPU. Docker containers have no resource constraints by default, so explicit limits and host capacity matter. Documentation describes platform behavior and configuration, but does not prove that a live deployment enforces a proposed policy.

Placement rule: Require the intended accelerator, sufficient device and host memory, compatible driver and runtime, artifact-storage reachability, and tested network capacity. Spread ready replicas across at least two host domains before making a two-domain availability claim. Two replicas on one host remain one host-failure domain. The lab's `domain` field is a deterministic abstraction, not a Kubernetes scheduler simulation.

Warm-up and readiness rule: A replacement passes through artifact download, digest verification, model load, compilation where required, cache warm-up, and an exact model-identity readiness probe. It contributes zero admission capacity while warming. A listening port or scheduled Pod alone is insufficient evidence of model readiness.

Drain and replacement rule: Mark a replica draining before route removal, stop new work, allow bounded in-flight work until the drain deadline, preserve telemetry, revoke its route, and then reclaim resources. Draining and failed replicas contribute zero capacity. Start a verified replacement, but do not count it until ready. Maintain at least four ready slots across the required domains.

Autoscaling rules: Use queue delay and admitted work units as leading signals, with saturation as corroborating evidence. Keep a minimum of four ready slots, cap the exercise fleet at twelve slots, and cap cost at 24 fictional cost units per hour. Allow two intervals for warm-up, require three stable intervals before scale-down, drain before removal, and retain the prior policy and capacity floor for rollback. Kubernetes HPA can use CPU, memory, or custom metrics to adjust replicas, but this lesson does not claim CPU alone predicts this workload's queue growth.

sections.title: Test shared-resource and failure isolation
paragraphs: Instructor narration: Failure testing asks what becomes unsafe, how far the effect travels, whether retries amplify demand, and whether recovery preserves identity and budgets. The complete activity tests ten concrete cases rather than treating replica count as availability evidence.

Ten synthetic failure cases: (1) A process crash removes one replica and permits retries only for safe in-flight work. (2) Device loss removes every replica using that device. (3) Host loss removes all replicas in that host domain. (4) Artifact-store delay blocks warming replacements without making them ready. (5) Network partition removes unreachable routes and invokes the dependency circuit. (6) Identity failure rejects protected requests without bypassing authorization. (7) Telemetry failure raises an alarm and leaves health evidence unknown rather than inventing capacity. (8) Queue pressure reaches its bound, sheds batch first, and rejects excess demand. (9) Malformed work is rejected before queueing and is not retried. (10) A bad model release fails identity or measured quality gates, remains unrouted, and triggers rollback to the verified prior release.

Required observations: Verify that readiness removes unsafe capacity, retries do not amplify load, queues remain bounded, one workload cannot starve another, model identity remains exact, and recovery does not accept stale or unverified artifacts. The immutable local tests cover warming, draining, and failed hosts; a shared failure domain; queue and deadline budgets; the cost ceiling; a positive changed input; unknown enums; malformed or unknown evidence; and bounded local temporary-fixture handling.

Fixture versus real integration: The Node 22 lab is a deterministic policy simulator. Hosts, status, slots, domains, costs, deadlines, and traffic observations are fixtures. It does not start containers, schedule Kubernetes Pods, allocate accelerators, download models, invoke provider APIs, measure live inference, verify a deployed security control, or approve production infrastructure. Real integration must observe the target scheduler, device plugin, runtime, artifact verification, readiness, cancellation propagation, routing, telemetry, quality evaluation, failure injection, and billing data. A fixture pass proves only that the local function handles supplied evidence consistently.

Independent learner variation, prediction first: Before running `changed-positive.json`, predict whether demand 9 should be admitted when two ready hosts each provide 4 slots and the queue limit is 2. The answer is not visible from nominal count alone, so list every gate. Explained answer: 4 + 4 = 8 ready slots, and 8 + 2 = 10 covers demand 9. Queue delay 40 ms plus service time 300 ms equals 340 ms, below the 1,000 ms deadline. Two ready domains meet the minimum of two. Cost 20 is below 24. The repaired decision is therefore ADMIT and APPROVE. A rejection indicates deny-all, stale capacity logic, or damage to another gate.

sections.title: Gate autoscaling and scale changes
paragraphs: Instructor narration: Autoscaling is a controlled change, not evidence of success by itself. Predeclare service, quality, cost, recovery, and rollback thresholds before comparing policies. Queue delay, concurrency, admitted work units, and saturation can be combined, while a stabilization window prevents a noisy sample from causing oscillation.

All values in the following comparison are fictional teaching data, not measured real-model or live-infrastructure performance. Predeclared service gates are: interactive p95 latency at most 700 ms, interactive queue delay at most 200 ms, and deadline 1,000 ms; batch p95 latency at most 5,000 ms, batch queue delay at most 2,000 ms, and deadline 30,000 ms. Allowed candidate rejection is 0 for steady and ramp, at most 1 batch request for skew, at most 1 request for burst, and 0 for failure demand up to retained capacity plus queue. Cost must be at most 24 units per hour. Recovery must restore the twelve-slot candidate within two intervals. Minimum safe ready capacity is four slots.

Predeclared synthetic quality gates apply to release `r17` with prompt contract `p4`, and are measured independently for baseline and candidate because concurrency, batching, routing, and timeouts may affect results even when model identity is unchanged. Interactive task success must be at least 95 correct out of 100 cases. Batch task success must be at least 188 correct out of 200 cases, which is 94 percent. Safety refusal correctness must be at least 49 correct out of 50 cases, which is 98 percent. Route-to-contract correctness must be 100 out of 100 cases. A changed release, prompt contract, denominator, or scoring rule invalidates comparison and makes quality UNKNOWN until reevaluated.

Steady comparison, demand 6: Baseline serves 6, rejects 0, records 0 ms queue delay, 420 ms interactive p95 latency, cost 12, and interactive quality 97/100. Candidate serves 6, rejects 0, records 0 ms queue delay, 390 ms p95 latency, cost 20, and quality 97/100. Both pass service and quality. The candidate has an 8-unit cost penalty, calculated as 20 - 12, but remains below the 24-unit ceiling.

Burst comparison, demand 13: Baseline ready capacity 8 plus queue 2 serves 10 and rejects 3 because 13 - 8 - 2 = 3. It records 410 ms queue delay and 1,120 ms interactive p95 latency, so it breaches the 200 ms queue and 700 ms latency gates. Candidate ready capacity 12 queues 1, serves 13, rejects 0, records 120 ms queue delay, 640 ms p95 latency, cost 20, and interactive quality 96/100. Candidate arithmetic is 13 - 12 = 1 queued unit, within the queue limit and rejection allowance. It passes all declared burst gates.

Ramp comparison, demands 6, 8, and 10: Baseline serves 6, 8, and 10 with queue delays 0, 80, and 260 ms, p95 latencies 420, 560, and 780 ms, and no rejection. Its third interval breaches both 200 ms queue and 700 ms latency gates. Candidate begins warming before the third interval and records ready capacities 8, 8, and 12 after the declared two-interval warm-up. It serves 6, 8, and 10 with queue delays 0, 70, and 60 ms, p95 latencies 400, 520, and 510 ms, no rejection, cost 20, and interactive quality 96/100. It passes because warming capacity is counted only after readiness.

Skewed comparison, interactive demand 7 plus batch demand 6: Baseline serves 6 interactive and 4 batch, queues 2 mixed requests, rejects 1 interactive and 2 batch, records 330 ms interactive queue delay and 810 ms interactive p95 latency, and therefore fails priority protection. Candidate routing serves all 7 interactive and 5 batch requests, rejects 1 batch request under its declared shedding rule, records 80 ms interactive queue delay, 500 ms interactive p95 latency, 900 ms batch queue delay, and 3,200 ms batch p95 latency. Candidate interactive quality is 96/100, batch quality is 189/200, and route correctness is 100/100. It passes every skew threshold because 189/200 = 94.5 percent and the sole rejection is lower-priority batch work.

Failure comparison, demand 6 after one host-domain loss: Baseline placed all ready replicas in the failed domain, retains 0 ready slots, serves 0, rejects 6, and has no valid latency result because no request completes. Candidate retains 4 ready slots in the second domain, queues 2, serves all 6, rejects 0, records 180 ms queue delay and 680 ms interactive p95 latency, and restores twelve ready slots after two intervals. Its safety quality result is 49/50 and route correctness is 100/100. It meets the 98 percent safety threshold exactly, the service thresholds, and the two-interval recovery objective.

Decision and rollback: The candidate passes the supplied synthetic service, quality, domain-isolation, cost, startup, recovery, and routing gates, so the artifact recommends only a staged fictional-policy decision. This is not live deployment approval. Roll back to the prior policy and four-slot floor if any measured quality denominator misses its threshold, release or prompt identity changes without reevaluation, cost exceeds 24, queue delay breaches for two intervals, readiness becomes unknown, route correctness is below 100/100, or recovery exceeds two intervals. Preserve the prior policy, route configuration, verified artifact identity, and capacity floor for reversal.

Rubric: A complete submission identifies the bottleneck and compares all eight alternatives; defines interactive, batch, and administrative admission, queue, deadline, retry, cancellation, circuit, shedding, and degraded-mode behavior; states placement, warm-up, readiness, drain, replacement, minimum, maximum-cost, and stabilization rules; reports all ten failure cases; computes all five traffic comparisons; evaluates service, quality, isolation, cost, startup, recovery, and rollback gates; repairs only the capacity defect; passes all eight immutable tests and the changed input; and distinguishes fixture evidence from integration evidence. Deny-all earns no repair credit because it fails the positive case.

Reflection guidance: CPU utilization may arrive too late when queue delay grows while a replacement is still warming. Queue delay or admitted work units can provide an earlier signal. A strong response explains lead time, links it to readiness delay, and states how stabilization avoids oscillation.

activity.title: Design and challenge a scaling policy
instructions: Use the supplied synthetic load result to identify one measured bottleneck and compare vertical, replica, sharded, batched, queued, cached, routed, and smaller-model options. Record quality, latency, failure, cost, and complexity effects.
Define per-workload admission, queue, deadline, retry, cancellation, circuit, shedding, and degraded-mode behavior. Explain why deny-all and admit-all are invalid.
Write placement, artifact warm-up, readiness, draining, replacement, minimum capacity, maximum cost, warm-up, and scale-down stabilization rules.
Create or review ten process, device, host, dependency, pressure, and bad-release failure cases with expected blast radius and recovery.

Calculate baseline and candidate results under steady, burst, ramp, skewed, and failure traffic. Apply the predeclared service, quality, cost, recovery, and rollback thresholds before issuing a reversible decision.

Prediction before execution: calculate `changed-positive.json` without running it. Then run the baseline and immutable tests. Repair only `src/policy.js`; do not modify tests, fixtures, schema validation, or the reference.

Run the changed input after repair and explain causally why it approves. Use `training/self-hosted-model-operations/scaling-failure-and-capacity-controls/lab/worked-artifact.json` as the answer key only after recording your prediction.
evidence: A bottleneck-to-pattern comparison with quality, latency, failure, cost, and complexity impacts.
An admission, backpressure, placement, warm-up, drain, autoscale, and degraded-mode policy.
A ten-case failure-isolation report and five-pattern baseline-candidate decision with numeric service, quality, cost, recovery, and rollback evidence.
A repaired `src/policy.js` that passes eight immutable tests and the changed input, with recorded starter and repaired output.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which autoscaling signal would arrive too late for your workload, and what leading signal should accompany it?

questions.prompt: What should drive selection of a scaling pattern?
choices: A measured bottleneck and service evidence
questions.explanation: Scaling should address the limiting resource without hiding other failures.

choices: Controls that bound or slow admitted work when downstream capacity is constrained
questions.explanation: Backpressure prevents upstream demand from overwhelming constrained components.

questions.prompt: When is a new replica ready?
choices: After exact artifact verification, load, warm-up, and readiness checks pass
questions.explanation: Useful capacity must be able to serve the intended verified model contract.

questions.prompt: Why can retries worsen an outage?
choices: Unbounded or unsafe retries multiply load and side effects during failure
questions.explanation: Retry amplification can turn partial failure into cascading overload.

questions.prompt: What should a failure-isolation test measure?
choices: Blast radius, removal from service, load amplification, state, identity, and recovery
questions.explanation: Isolation claims require observed impact and controlled recovery.

questions.prompt: What makes an autoscaling policy reversible?
choices: A preserved prior policy, safe floor, tested rollback, and exact change evidence
questions.explanation: A retained verified baseline and tested rollback support rapid reversal.

concurrency, rejection, quality, and cost.

ten milliseconds. These observations
